doc.title: Al Gafa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2023

chapter: Playboy Club and the working life
title: Playboy Club trio with Monty Alexander and Bob Cranshaw
summary: At the Playboy Club he was musically beaten up nightly by Alexander and Cranshaw, learning harmony and tunes on the job.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: on songs, no. I didn’t work on songs. But when I first started playing I worked at — I got a job at the Playboy Club. It came through another guitar player who was leaving and it was a trio job, it was guitar, bass, and piano. The piano player was Monty Alexander and the bass player was Bob Cranshaw. And the guitar player was me. I thought I knew something about the guitar from doing all that studying and playing. But when I got in that jazz situation, those two guys used to beat me up physically — musically — every night, because they were such proficient musicians. They were just off the — I couldn’t figure — I used to go home at night and figure out where they knocked me out in every tune that they knocked me out and there was a regularity there. So as for learning tunes I learned those kind of tunes through them. And I learned — I didn’t learn all the different — I learned different directions to take with harmonies and changes. And that improved — I started to be able to incorporate some of the studies that I did from clarinet and violin just because I had the technique to manipulate between changes. So it was really on-the- job training but heavy on-the-job training by good trainers. That’s how I began.
If they called a tune one night let’s say “What a Difference a Day Makes” and you didn’t know it, so you went home to learn it, first of all how did you access that tune? Did you have fake books?

Okay let me — I have fairly decent ears so when we’re on a session and somebody plays something I can anticipate where the bass line is going. It’s very important for me, the bass line is the key to the thing. And so you hear the harmony on the top, you hear the bass line on the bottom, you almost know where the next change is going to go. So I can anticipate where it’s going to go and I’m ready for it. But Bob and Monty, every once in a while would change the direction and I’d be playing where I think it would go and they’d be playing where they wanted to go. So that’s the kind of studying I had to go home — I didn’t have to learn those tunes. And I knew tons of tunes because I used to play jobs with another guitar player and his wife who was a singer, and you know singers sing fifty tunes a night and so your repertoire builds on the past.
Yes and you often learn them in different keys depending on if it’s a guy or a girl.
